newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Unisource strategy intact after Telefonica jolt.
newsitem.headline: Unisource strategy intact after Telefonica jolt.

text.p: Telecommunications joint venture Unisource is still in shape to compete fully with its main rivals, despite news a key member was preparing to leave the group, a senior Unisource spokesman said on Friday.

The Unisource telecoms venture, headquartered in the Netherlands, groups Koninklijke PTT Nederland, Telia of Sweden, Swiss Telecom PTT and Telefonica of Spain which earlier announced an alliance with a British/U.S. combination.

Unisource itself has a business communications joint venture with AT & T Corp called AT&T Unisource, which the spokesman said remained on track after Telefonica's alliance with MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc.
"It's not, as the Financial Times said, the ruination of AT&T Unisource at all," said Ben Verwaayen, head of KPN's telecom arm and chairman of AT&T Unisource's supervisory board.
"We have very ambitious plans to go forward and there's absolutely no doubt in my mind that the AT&T Unisource combination is well on track," he added.

Verwaayen said Unisource felt in no way overawed by its main rivals, Global One -- the alliance of Deutsche Telekom AG , France Telecom and Sprint Corp -- and Concert -- the grouping of British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp.

"We presently win 63 percent of all the voice contracts that have a pan-European reach," said Verwaayen, dismissing speculation by analysts that the Telefonica move could lead to Unisource trailing the main competition. "I don't know what trailing behind is," he added.
He was equally short with speculation that AT&T could find the remaining interests in Unisource unappealing, putting the venture in a weak position.
"Happily I have in front of me some signed letters from John Walter, the CEO of AT&T saying that the commitment to Unisource and the way forward is unshocked by these events," he said.
"It remains fully in place and has reason to remain in place because we're doing quite well in the market," Verwaayen said.
He said the move reflected a change in the Telefonica strategy but acknowledged that it had denied Unisource potential access to Latin American telecommunications markets.

"The previous management was seeking an integration of their activities in Europe. The present management has said they will be satisfied by a strong position domestically with a focus in their growth potential to Latin America," said Verwaayen.

"We've lost potential access to that (Latin American) market, no doubt about it. But on the other hand there are more opportunities to go to that market. How and where are interesting questions to be answered later," said Verwaayen.
He said Unisource wanted to sit down with Telefonica and settle issues arising from the split out of court, although he did not rule out the possibility of a law suit.
"There is a breach of contract. We can settle with them out of court, but if necessary will take other steps," he said.
He declined to speculate on talk that Unisource was lining up STET of Italy as a possible replacement for Telefonica.

"We don't exclude the entrance of a fourth partner. We will be carefully selecting the opportunities. There have been many parties in the past who have shown interest in joining us but we're absolutely not going to hurry," he said.
Verwaayen added that Unisource would be holding a news conference in the Netherlands on April 21 to underline the commitment of AT&T to the venture.

"The commitment of AT&T is there 100 percent. Our strategy remains in place. It's very unfortunate that we've lost our friends from Telefonica but it's their decision, their change of policy, we continue on track," Verwaayen said.
